required_recommendations: Diagnose syncope caused by acute bilateral pulmonary embolism, intermediate-high risk by ESC 2019 (haemodynamically stable, sPESI 1 or more, RV dysfunction on echocardiography and CT, raised troponin), provoked by right knee arthroplasty 18 days ago
Admit to a monitored bed (high-dependency or step-down unit) for continuous monitoring of blood pressure, heart rhythm and oxygenation over the first days; do not discharge
Start therapeutic parenteral anticoagulation without delay: weight-based LMWH (preferred, ESC 2019), or an unfractionated heparin infusion if reperfusion becomes likely or CrCl falls below 30 mL/min

Plan rescue reperfusion if she deteriorates haemodynamically; systemic thrombolysis is contraindicated within 3 weeks of major surgery (ESC 2019), so the rescue options are catheter-directed treatment or surgical embolectomy, to be arranged with the PE response team in advance
Stop aspirin when therapeutic anticoagulation starts: its only indication was venous thromboprophylaxis and the combination adds bleeding risk
Give supplemental oxygen when SpO2 is below 90% (ESC 2019), preferring high-flow nasal oxygen to positive-pressure ventilation, which can worsen RV failure

Continue anticoagulation with a DOAC (apixaban or rivaroxaban) after the initial parenteral phase, for 3 months, since the PE was provoked by a major transient risk factor (ESC 2019 Class I); thrombophilia testing is not indicated for provoked VTE (NICE NG158)

Do not withhold metformin for the contrast alone (eGFR about 79 mL/min/1.73 m2, no AKI; ACR Manual on Contrast Media); withhold it while she is hypoxaemic with lactate 2.8 mmol/L, cover glucose with insulin as needed, and restart once she is stable
Advise no driving until the pulmonary embolism is treated and she is free of symptoms (ESC 2018 driving advice after syncope with a treated cause)

differential.key_features: Troponin I 0.18 ng/mL with precordial T-wave inversion could suggest NSTEMI, but there is no ST deviation, CK-MB is normal, the T-wave inversion with S1Q3T3, right axis and incomplete RBBB is a right-heart strain pattern, LV wall motion is normal on echocardiography, and CT confirms bilateral PE with RV strain.

A brief prodrome ('room closing in') was reported, but there was no trigger, she remains tachycardic and hypoxaemic, and the echocardiogram and CT pulmonary angiogram show bilateral PE with RV pressure overload.
Tachycardia raised the question of an arrhythmia, but 24 h of telemetry shows only sinus tachycardia, with no AF, flutter, SVT, VT, AV block or pause.

The syncope occurred while standing, but persistent tachycardia and hypoxaemia at rest, pleuritic pain and the RV pressure overload on echocardiography and CT are not explained by orthostatic hypotension.

Post-operative dehydration or bleeding could cause syncope, but BUN and creatinine are normal, haemoglobin 11.4 g/dL is in keeping with post-operative anaemia rather than acute haemorrhage, and the CT shows bilateral PE with RV strain.

general.query: syncope initial evaluation and risk stratification

results.key_finding: Initial evaluation comprises history, physical examination including supine and standing blood pressure, and a 12-lead ECG. High-risk features (syncope during exertion or supine, palpitations before the event, known structural or coronary disease, family history of sudden death under 40, high-risk ECG findings) call for early in-hospital evaluation with immediate ECG monitoring. Echocardiography is indicated when structural heart disease is known or suspected; EEG, brain imaging and routine laboratory panels are not recommended without a specific indication.
results.title: 2018 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope (Brignole M et al., Eur Heart J 2018;39:1883-1948)

results.key_finding: Risk stratification at the initial evaluation separates patients needing in-hospital monitoring and cardiac testing from those suitable for outpatient evaluation; targeted rather than routine blood testing is advised.
results.title: 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the evaluation and management of patients with syncope (Shen WK et al.)

general.summary: Guidelines base syncope work-up on the initial evaluation (history, examination, orthostatic BP, 12-lead ECG) and risk stratification; high-risk patients receive in-hospital ECG monitoring and targeted cardiac testing.

clinical_pearls: PE presenting with syncope carries a higher short-term risk than PE without syncope; consider PE in any recently operated patient with unexplained syncope, tachycardia and hypoxaemia
The S1Q3T3 pattern is neither sensitive nor specific for PE, but with the clinical probability and the RV findings it directs the work-up
McConnell sign (mid RV free-wall akinesis with a preserved apex) supports acute RV pressure overload
At high clinical probability the D-dimer is skipped and CT pulmonary angiography is performed directly; after recent surgery the D-dimer is also non-specific
Major surgery within 3 weeks contraindicates systemic thrombolysis; plan catheter-directed or surgical rescue in advance
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Six required steps (ECG, troponin/BNP/pregnancy test, TTE, telemetry, CT pulmonary angiography, medication review) and three red herrings; the troponin and precordial T-wave inversion invite an ACS diagnosis, the post-operative context invites dismissal of calf tenderness and dyspnoea, and the rescue plan must account for the recent surgery.

social_history.occupation: Elementary school teacher, currently on medical leave following surgery

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Denise Carter is a 48-year-old African American woman with hypertension, obesity, and type 2 diabetes who presents to the emergency department after a sudden witnessed syncopal episode at home approximately 30 minutes ago. Her husband reports that she was standing at the kitchen counter approximately 40 minutes after getting up from bed when she suddenly turned pale, stated she felt 'like the room was closing in,' and collapsed to the floor within seconds; she did not strike her head. He estimates she was unresponsive for approximately 45 to 60 seconds, after which she spontaneously regained consciousness and was immediately alert and oriented. He did not observe any convulsive limb movements, tongue biting, or incontinence. Emergency medical services were called; on arrival, they recorded an oxygen saturation of 89% on room air and a heart rate of 124 bpm. She was given supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula with improvement in saturation to 94%. She denies any prior similar episode. She reports that over the past 3 to 4 days she has experienced progressive mild right-sided pleuritic chest discomfort that she attributed to a 'pulled muscle' from using her walker, and she has noticed increasing shortness of breath with minimal exertion, which she assumed was deconditioning from her surgery 18 days ago. She denies prior cardiac history, palpitations, or arrhythmia. She has been largely immobile since her total knee arthroplasty, spending most of her time in a recliner and making short trips to the bathroom with her walker. Her orthopedic surgeon discharged her on aspirin 81 mg daily for DVT prophylaxis per institutional protocol, though she acknowledges she missed her aspirin dose three times in the past week. She has no family history of clotting disorders, though her mother had a DVT after a long flight. On review of systems, she denies fever, hemoptysis, leg ulcers, or prior blood clots. She endorses mild right calf tenderness she attributed to post-operative swelling.

neurological_exam.additional: No tongue laceration or lateral tongue bite marks. No urinary incontinence during the episode per husband's report. Right knee with a healing incision, staples removed, and mild erythema at the incision site, without fluctuance, warmth exceeding that expected, or signs of wound infection. Right calf mildly tender to palpation. Mild bilateral ankle edema, right greater than left. Homans' sign negative (a sign of low sensitivity).
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing intact bilaterally without dysmetria or intention tremor. Heel-to-shin on left intact. Rapid alternating movements normal.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: CN II: Visual fields full to confrontation bilaterally. Pupils equal, round, reactive to light 3mm to 2mm bilaterally. No papilledema on fundoscopic exam. CN III/IV/VI: Extraocular movements intact, no nystagmus or diplopia. CN V: Facial sensation intact in all three divisions. Masseter and pterygoid strength symmetric. CN VII: Face symmetric at rest and with voluntary movement. CN VIII: Hearing grossly intact bilaterally to finger rub. CN IX/X: Palate elevates symmetrically, gag intact bilaterally. CN XI: Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. CN XII: Tongue protrudes midline, no fasciculations or atrophy.
neurological_exam.gait: Unable to perform tandem gait due to post-surgical limitations. Ambulates with walker; gait is antalgic on the right but steady. Romberg not formally tested given mobility limitations.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Glasgow Coma Scale 15. Speech fluent without dysarthria or aphasia. Attention intact. Recall 3/3 objects at 5 minutes. No confusion or post-ictal state at the time of evaluation, approximately 40 minutes after the syncopal episode.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal in upper extremities. Right lower extremity with expected post-surgical swelling. Tone normal and symmetric, no rigidity or spasticity. Strength 5/5 in bilateral upper extremities and left lower extremity; right lower extremity limited by pain (unable to fully assess). No pronator drift. No tremor at rest or with posture.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ on the left (right deferred due to surgical site). Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor (downgoing) bilaterally. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, and vibration intact in bilateral upper extremities and left lower extremity. Right lower extremity sensation grossly intact to light touch despite post-surgical swelling.
